Architecture: Hybrid R6+S7 design - S7 data: Immutable value types (token, call_argument, variable_assignment, function_signature, AST nodes) - R6 state machines: Mutable objects manage internal state (ParserState, future: LinterFileCache) - Type-safe boundaries: R6 constructors validate S7 inputs, R6 methods return S7 outputs hybrid? - S7 excels immutable data structures value semantics - R6 excels mutable state machines reference semantics - Forcing S7 onto mutable state creates awkward designs (performance overhead, complexity) - Using right tool problem important architectural purity Example (ParserState): - Stores list S7 token objects - Mutates position parsing (advance() called 15-20 times) - Returns S7 tokens current() method - Validates S7 inputs construction, provides bounds checking Future: R6 method typing support planned 2.0, pending user demand. text: rdoc uses S7 objects throughout. Tests leverage S7’s built-equality semantics instead property--property assertions. ✅ PREFERRED (declarative, complete): ⚠️ USE SPARINGLY (checking 1-2 specific fields): Benefits: - Declarative: Shows complete expected state glance - Robust: Catches properties added/removed/changed - Self-documenting: Clear complete object - Better diffs: testthat shows full object diff failure - Type-safe: Can’t forget assert property Real example: refactoring test-type-parser.R use object equality, tests caught incorrect position values property-based tests never checked. prevented silent bugs position tracking. use property assertions: - Checking type/class object (e.g., @type EOF tokens value/position don’t matter) - Testing one specific field isolation - Objects complex fields hard construct (e.g., XML nodes) Going forward: new S7 tests use object equality default. Property assertions justified comments.

Add context-aware explanation   union_analysis <- analyze_union_incompatibility(actual_display, expected_type)    if (!is.null(union_analysis$scenario) && union_analysis$scenario == "partial") {     # what: Design Decision: R6 for State Machines, S7 for Data Structures
title: rdoc Development Logbook
text: Problem: formalizing call arguments, tokens, variable assignments S7 (Phases 29-31), question arose: formalize parser state S7 complete type system formalization? Parser state fundamentally different data structures ’d formalized: - Data structures (token, call_argument): Created , immutable, passed around - Parser state: Created , mutates constantly (advance() called 15-20 times per parse) Forcing S7 (value semantics) onto inherently mutable state created awkward designs. Exploration Process: Four approaches considered: Pro: Zero performance overhead (mutate place) Con: Validation construction, still corrupt state Pro: Functional purity, fully testable Con: Every parse function must change, high refactor cost, breaks clean recursive structure Pro: Type-safe functions, similar API Con: Unusual pattern, parse functions change ($ → @) Pro: Minimal changes, overhead Con: formalized type system, just defensive programming None felt right. forcing S7 onto wrong problem. Insight: State machines ≠ Data structures Solution: Hybrid architecture - use R6 S7 strengths. Architecture: R6 Implementation: Benefits: - ✅ Semantic correctness: R6 designed mutable state machines - ✅ Zero performance overhead: Mutate place, object creation - ✅ Encapsulation: Private fields protect internal state - ✅ Type-safe boundaries: R6 validates S7 inputs, returns S7 outputs - ✅ Zero API changes: Parser interface stays parser$current() - ✅ Honest architecture: Acknowledges different needs (data vs. state)
code: Data Layer (S7 - Immutable): ├── token                    # Lexer output ├── call_argument            # Function call args ├── variable_assignment      # Variable tracking ├── function_signature       # Type signatures └── AST nodes               # Type syntax AST  State Machines (R6 - Mutable): ├── ParserState             # Token stream parser └── [Future] LinterFileCache # Multi-pass type cache  Interaction Contract: - R6 constructors validate S7 inputs - R6 methods return S7 outputs - Type-safe boundaries enforced ParserState <- R6::R6Class(   "ParserState",   private = list(     tokens = NULL,      # List of S7 token objects     position = NULL,      check_bounds = function() {       if (private$position < 1 || private$position > length(private$tokens)) {         stop(sprintf("Position %d out of bounds", private$position))       }     }   ),    public = list(     initialize = function(tokens) {       # Validate S7 inputs       if (!all(vapply(tokens, function(t) S7::S7_inherits(t, token), logical(1)))) {         stop("All tokens must be S7 token objects")       }       private$tokens <- tokens       private$position <- 1L     },      current = function() {       private$check_bounds()       private$tokens[[private$position]]  # Returns S7 token     },      advance = function() {       if (private$position < length(private$tokens)) {         private$position <- private$position + 1L       }       private$check_bounds()       private$tokens[[private$position]]  # Returns S7 token     }   ) )  # S7 wrapper for type-safe composition parser_state <- S7::new_S3_class("ParserState")

Internal R6 simple: ParserState ~100 lines, low risk 5. Pragmatic: Right tool job (R6 state), don’t -commit User perspective: “rdoc types functions using roxygen2 tags. uses R6 internally performance, doesn’t type R6 yet.” Future path: users request R6 typing rdoc gains traction, add minimal R6 support 2.0. Documentation: Added CLAUDE.md: Key Insight: everything S7. Choosing right tool problem important architectural purity. State machines (mutable, imperative) need different abstractions data structures (immutable, declarative). R6 S7 complement perfectly used intended purposes. mirrors mature ecosystems: - Rust: Immutable default, mut need - Haskell: Pure functional, IORef mutable state - Clojure: Immutable data, atoms coordinated state rdoc’s hybrid R6+S7 architecture follows pattern: immutable data (S7) mutable state machines (R6) semantically appropriate. text: Problem: [N] syntax length constraints (e.g., numeric[1] scalars) fought R’s vectorized nature created user confusion. Solution: Removed length constraint support, keeping element type constraints <type> generics. Rationale: - R fundamentally vectorized: Fighting creates friction R’s core design philosophy - Incomplete implementation: Static analysis couldn’t reliably check length constructed vectors (c(1, 2)) - Implementation complexity: Required @length_constraint property, actual_length parameter threading, special-case logic throughout codebase - User confusion: Scalars work literals expressions - inconsistent behavior worse behavior - truly R-like: R doesn’t distinguish scalars length-1 vectors type level Removed: - [N] syntax length constraints (e.g., numeric[1], character[5]) - @length_constraint property type_ref S7 class - check_length_constraint() function - actual_length parameter types_compatible() - length constraint parsing logic parse_type_constraints() - 22+ test files updated, test-linter-bracket-syntax.R → test-element-types.R Kept: - Element type constraints: list<integer> generic types - type system features (unions, external types, NULL safety, etc.) Key Insight: Sometimes removing feature makes system better. R’s vectorization core strength - type checking embrace , fight . Accept imprecision vector lengths rather provide inconsistent behavior. Enabled: - Cleaner, simpler type system aligned R’s philosophy - Removed 500+ lines constraint-checking code - Reduced cognitive load users (one less syntax learn) - Better alignment R developers actually think types Migration Path: Users : - Remove [N] type annotations - Accept numeric means “numeric vector length” - Use prose documentation scalar requirements (just like base R) - Rely runtime checks length validation needed
